narrative: The model estimates a 58% chance that you will leave your job, meaning leaving is somewhat more likely than staying; the promotion was denied because that retention risk was judged too high, not because your ability was rejected. The most influential signal was your total work experience of 1–5 years. This pushed toward staying, since it matches about half of employees predicted to stay. Your monthly salary of 6k–10k SAR was the second most influential signal and also pushed toward staying; it is the most common salary band among employees predicted to stay. The third signal was difficulty getting involved in job decisions and expressing opinions. This pushed toward leaving, and it is unusual among employees predicted to stay—only about one in ten reported this difficulty. Even though experience and salary point toward stability, the overall picture includes low emotional commitment, low job support, little recognition, no bonus or medical insurance, physical stress, psychological exhaustion, felt job instability, and general dissatisfaction; together these keep the estimated leaving risk above half. The organization should treat 58% as a warning, not a certainty: discuss your concerns, improve involvement and recognition, clarify support and promotion criteria, and review pay and benefits. You should use that conversation to say what would make you stay and whether the denied promotion changes your plans.
